newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Opponents urge Kabila to allow U.N. massacre probe.
newsitem.headline: Opponents urge Kabila to allow U.N. massacre probe.

text.p: Congo's opposition urged President Laurent Kabila on Tuesday to allow U.N. investigators free access to alleged refugee massacre sites, and said they were prepared to guide the U.N. there themselves.
Opposition leader Joseph Olenghankoy told a news conference he feared Kabila could have something to hide.

"The probe must be conducted. If Kabila keeps hesitating, we will take the investigators wherever they would like to go in this country. We want some clarification. We don't want the country's image to be stained," he said.
An advance U.N. team said on Sunday Kabila's government had rejected two terms for the investigation that were set down in April in a resolution of the U.N. human rights commission.
Kabila's Tutsi-dominated Alliance forces and their allies, who overthrew president Mobutu Sese Seko in May after a seven- month campaign, have been accused of massacring Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Kabila has denied the allegations but has blocked attempts by the investigators to go ahead with the probe.
At least one million Rwandan Hutus, including those who were responsible for the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis in Rwanda, fled into former Zaire in 1994.
Up to 800,000 returned home when Kabila's rebels overran their refugee camps in the early stage of the rebellion last year. Some died from exhaustion or hunger as they were fleeing the war zone.
But over 100,000 are still reported missing by U.N. refugee officials.
"When we see Kabila's attitude (towards the U.N. team), we ask ourselves a lot of questions," Olenghankoy said.
He said that Kabila was a proxy ruler because the Democratic Republic of Congo was ruled from Rwanda and Uganda.
"We have on our soil occupation foreign troops that the current head of state has hired. But we don't know the terms of the agreement he reached with his (foreign) friends," Olenghankoy said.
Many Congolese say Rwandan, Burundian and Ugandian soldiers are in the ranks of Kabila's forces, which he denies.
Olenghankoy called unsuccesfully for anti-government demonstrations on Monday to mar Independence Day festivities.
